items.title: Effectiveness of Integration of Gamification and Rewards for Learner Engagement in Online and Distance Learning Contexts
items.abstract: Gamification is widely used to enhance learner engagement and motivation in online and distance learning (ODL) contexts, however, its interaction with reward mechanisms remains underexplored. This study examined the combined role of gamification and rewards as a motivational strategy in higher education ODL contexts using a descriptive survey design with a sample of 239 higher education students. Descriptive and inferential analyses were conducted, including correlation and multiple regression techniques. Pearson correlation analysis indicated that gamification and rewards were both positively correlated with learner engagement (r = .35 and r = .61, respectively; p < .01), and gamification was also moderately correlated with rewards (r = .52, p < .01). Multiple regression analysis revealed that gamification and rewards jointly explained a substantial proportion of the variance in learner engagement (R² = .38, adjusted R² = .37, F (2, 236) = 70.65, p < .001). However, when examined simultaneously, rewards emerged as a significant predictor of engagement (β = .59, p < .001), whereas gamification did not demonstrate a significant independent effect (β = .05, p = .418). These findings suggest that while gamification is associated with engagement, rewards also play a central role in predicting learner engagement within gamified ODL contexts. The proposed integrative perspective offers practical implications for instructional designers and ODL providers seeking to develop sustainable engagement strategies.

items.title: Effects of AI-assisted case discussion and virtual patient consultation on medical students’ learning outcomes
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) holds broad application prospects in medical education; however, systematic empirical evidence regarding its effectiveness in facilitating case discussions and virtual patient consultation remains scarce. This study recruited undergraduate medical students and conducted experiments to examine the pedagogical effects of AI-assisted case discussion and virtual consultation. Methods A total of 207 medical undergraduates participated in this study. Using the self-developed intelligent experimental platform, medical students engaged in AI-assisted case discussion and virtual consultation. Experiment 1 employed a single-factor, three-level between-subjects design to compare the effects of AI-assisted case discussion, peer case discussion, and a lecture-only control condition on medical students’ knowledge acquisition, intrinsic motivation, and interaction quality. Experiment 2 utilized a single-factor, four-level between-subjects design to examine the effects of virtual patient consultation and the sequencing of AI-assisted case discussion and virtual consultation on medical students’ knowledge acquisition, intrinsic motivation, and consultation process quality. The control group participants were the same individuals across both experiments. Results Results indicated that the AI-assisted case discussion group achieved significantly higher knowledge scores than the control group. The virtual consultation group, the consultation-then-discussion group, and the discussion-then-consultation group all outperformed the control group in knowledge acquisition. The discussion-then-consultation group demonstrated higher intrinsic motivation and consultation comprehensiveness, yet exhibited lower empathy than the virtual consultation group. Conclusions These findings suggest that both AI-assisted case discussion and virtual patient consultation can effectively enhance medical students’ knowledge acquisition compared with learning by watching instructional videos only, while different intervention sequences exert differential effects on intrinsic motivation, consultation comprehensiveness, and empathy. The results provide theoretical foundations and practical guidance for AI-empowered medical education.

items.title: EFL Students’ Perception and Motivation toward BBC News Videos for Autonomous Listening Activity
items.abstract: Authentic digital materials offer students learning English as a foreign language (EFL) opportunities to practice listening outside the classroom. This study examined undergraduates’ perceptions of BBC News videos on YouTube and their motivation to use them for autonomous listening at the English Department of Universitas Negeri Padang. The descriptive cross-sectional survey involved 43 second-year students who had completed the Intermediate Listening course and used BBC News videos for independent listening practice. Responses to a 28-item questionnaire administered via Google Forms were summarized using frequencies, percentages, and means. The overall mean score of 3.20 corresponded to the agreement category. Perceived ease of use had the highest mean (3.41), followed by extrinsic motivation (3.23), intrinsic motivation (3.22), and perceived usefulness (3.17). Perceived enjoyment had the lowest mean (2.95), which remained in the positive range. These findings suggest that students view BBC News videos as an accessible source of authentic spoken English for autonomous listening. Selecting suitable topics and providing guidance on challenging news content may improve students’ experience with these materials.

items.title: Epistemic coordination systems for scientific laboratories: Protocol for a provenance-first scoping review and systematic map
items.abstract: Scientific laboratories are rapidly adopting artificial intelligence tools, electronic laboratory notebooks, automated workflows, and digital twins. Yet, these typically operate as isolated components rather than as parts of a coherent laboratory-scale knowledge infrastructure. We use the term Epistemic Coordination Systems (ECS) to refer to the class of human-governed systems that coordinate laboratory memory, provenance, tacit knowledge, negative laboratory results, external evidence, AI-supported synthesis, verification status, and human judgment gates. The literature needed to conceptualize ECS exists but is fragmented across streams ranging from distributed cognition and transactive memory to retrieval-augmented generation, AI governance, and connected laboratories. This protocol specifies a scoping review with systematic mapping that will integrate these streams: eligibility follows a Population-Concept-Context framework centered on scientific laboratories; searches cover seven bibliographic and preprint sources plus official standards sources, with search strings calibrated against a documented 212-record seed corpus and peer reviewed before execution; screening proceeds in two stages, and a second reviewer independently re-screens at least 20 percent of records at each stage as a reliability check. From every included source, sixteen predefined data fields are extracted. Synthesis then produces four outputs: a map of the literature streams, a taxonomy of ECS components, distinctions between ECS and adjacent systems, and an initial set of design requirements and evaluation dimensions. Distinctively, the protocol is provenance-first: it applies to its own conduct the epistemic-coordination principles it studies, through bounded and non-binding AI assistance, human verification of every decision and claim, dedicated AI-provenance and human-override logs, and claim-source mapping. The protocol was registered before formal searches (OSF Registries; DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/WGMUY ; July 5, 2026).

items.title: EvoMisty: Building, Optimizing, and Evolving Capabilities on a Social Robot
items.abstract: Social robots face diverse and changing tasks in companionship and education. LLM-based methods can generate task programs, but they still rely on manually developed control interfaces and predefined capabilities. They also lack a general mechanism to optimize completed tasks based on user-specified metrics and reuse performance improvements across tasks.We present EvoMisty, a plugin-based framework that enables coding agents to build and continually improve robot capabilities. EvoMisty builds a control program from official documentation and verifies candidate capabilities on a physical robot. Verified capabilities are stored in an atomic capability library and combined with existing skills to solve tasks. After task completion, EvoMisty can collect execution data, measure user-specified metrics, and iteratively improve task programs. It then distills reusable skills from final solutions into a skill library for future tasks.We evaluate EvoMisty on a physical Misty II robot using Claude Code and Codex. The two agents construct 109 and 107 verified atomic capabilities, respectively. Both complete all 28 AutoMisty benchmark tasks and seven additional tasks beyond AutoMisty's capabilities. Optimization improves all seven evaluated metrics across five tasks. For example, dialogue response latency decreases by 52% and 71%, respectively. Reusing skills from one optimized dialogue task reduces latency by 33% to 72% in three other dialogue tasks without further optimization. All code and experimental videos will be publicly released through the webpage: https://wangxiaoshawn.github.io/projects/evomisty/index.html

items.title: From AI-Assisted to Autonomous Cybersecurity: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving cybersecurity from rule-based and analyst-driven operations towards agentic and potentially autonomous cyber defence. Existing reviews mostly classify models, datasets, or applications, and they rarely separate the sophistication of an AI model from the authority it holds to act. This article presents a structured review of peer-reviewed literature and develops a conceptual framework that treats autonomy and operational assurance as interdependent properties of the complete defensive system. The presented framework has four components: a five-dimension taxonomy covering security function, autonomy maturity, AI architecture, operational capability, and governance; a five-level autonomy maturity model (A0–A4) defined by decision authority, execution permission, and human role; a governance-by-design architecture with a runtime policy decision point and risk-sensitive delegation; and an evaluation framework that adds decision quality, unsafe action rate, intervention frequency, policy compliance, and verification success to conventional detection metrics. A research roadmap to 2033 sets out measurement, architectural, and assurance priorities. The contributions are conceptual and methodological and are not empirically validated. The article specifies the coding evidence and evaluation designs required for that validation. The framework gives researchers and practitioners a shared vocabulary for classifying, procuring, and governing AI-enabled cyber defence.

items.title: From data‑driven smart cities to AI‑driven urban governance: reallocating human–AI roles through an expert Delphi study
items.abstract: South Korea’s national urban policy is undergoing a third paradigm shift, from smart cities to AI cities, following the earlier transition from ubiquitous cities to smart cities. This shift reframes urban governance from optimization and control to autonomy and uncertainty, as AI moves from a data-processing tool toward an autonomous actor. Existing research has focused predominantly on data management, leaving human–AI authority redistribution underexamined. This study addresses this gap through a modified three-round Delphi survey of eleven domain experts. Expert consensus was high and broad (39 of 40 items, 97.5%), but convergence did not always signify strong endorsement: agreement centered on data governance, transparency, and prior definition of accountability as requirements for delegation, while expert rationales qualified support for experimentation and regulatory sandboxes, and governance reform remained contested. Support for human final authority coexisted with acceptance of routine automation, indicating that the human–AI boundary depends on decision consequences rather than a citywide automation level. Integrating levels-of-automation theory, Responsible AI, and Meaningful Human Control, the study proposes Responsible Autonomy and a provisional five-level AI-City Autonomy Level taxonomy calibrating AI autonomy against human oversight (HITL/HOTL), using the Delphi findings to specify conditions for delegation rather than to assign urban functions to levels.

items.title: From dyad to triad: human–AI collaboration and the changing roles of teachers and learners in formal education
items.abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into education presents opportunities alongside challenges, particularly in formal education, where the interaction between teachers and learners is increasingly extended by AI systems. Through dynamic, language-based contributions to instructional processes, AI can support understanding, engagement, and reflection, yet it may also promote cognitive offloading, deskilling, and overreliance on fluent but potentially flawed outputs. This theoretical article brings together perspectives on how generative AI reshapes teaching and learning, using school-based teaching as a paradigmatic case. It argues that the core educational significance of generative AI lies in its interactional and epistemic role and describes how the interpersonal teacher–learner dyad is extended into a triad of teachers, learners, and AI systems. Building on, but not replicating, the didactic triangle, this triadic model highlights the role of AI in learning processes: human and AI contributions are closely intertwined, while, as the article argues from an educational perspective, epistemic responsibility remains with human actors. Drawing on research on processing fluency, trust calibration, and metacognition, the article elaborates mechanisms of human–AI interaction, such as the epistemic evaluation of outputs, trust formation, and metacognitive regulation, with emphasis on the tension between apparent plausibility and actual accuracy. In addition to the triadic model, the article introduces two constructs: generative–evaluative reasoning, which captures the coupled demands of prompt formulation and critical output evaluation in recursive chatbot interactions, and AI usage competency, an integrative model of cognitive, attitudinal, motivational-volitional, and social dispositions for effective and responsible AI use. It further describes the problem of reciprocal AI delegation (RAID), a risk condition in which the design and the completion of learning tasks are delegated to AI. These considerations are condensed into four propositions with predictions to guide future research linking output characteristics, prior knowledge, modes of interaction, learning, and teachers’ diagnostic judgments. The article thus offers a perspective on the changing roles of teachers, learners, and AI and a basis for empirical research, for instructional designs that sustain deep cognitive engagement, and for the provision of suitable AI-based assistance systems in teaching and learning.

items.title: From resistance to integration: the dynamic evolution and enhancement of college English learner engagement in the digital textbook context — a narrative tracking study
items.abstract: The widespread adoption of digital textbooks offers unprecedented opportunities for longitudinal inquiry into learner engagement in university English education. This study employed a narrative inquiry paradigm to track 20 undergraduates’ engagement across one semester (six units, 16 weeks) using the Finance English Integrated Course digital textbook. Data included three waves of semi-structured narrative interviews (N = 60), 16-week learning logs and weekly questionnaires, plus platform behavioral logs from Unipus AI. Four-dimensional engagement (behavioral, cognitive, affective, interactive) was analyzed. Key findings: (1) Students’ experiential trajectories followed a three-phase pattern—Resistance (U1–U2), Adaptation (U3–U4), and Integration (U5–U6); “pleasant routine” dominated (42.5%), but “challenging efforts” and “aesthetic peak” combined only 32.5%, revealing a “convenience-induced superficial engagement” paradox. (2) Four-dimensional engagement showed “asynchronous evolution”: affective engagement improved earliest (around U3), cognitive engagement latest (around U5), behavioral engagement was most variable, and interactive engagement was most agentic—challenging the unitary engagement assumption in prior literature. (3) Three conceptual propositions were inductively derived—the Three-Phase Digital Textbook Adaptation Engagement Model, the Asynchronous Four-Dimensional Engagement Evolution framework, and the Agency-Engagement Feedback Cycle of Platform Feature Exploration—which are offered as empirically grounded hypotheses for future testing rather than as established theories. Four reform pathways are proposed as evidence-informed implications for practice: digital textbook interface optimization, classroom instructional design, multi-dimensional assessment mechanisms, and platform technical support.

items.title: Generalizing Agentic Robotics via Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
items.abstract: Building general-purpose robots is a central goal in robotics. Agentic robotics pursues this goal with planners that control robots through tool calls. However, existing methods either rely on proprietary models accessed through APIs, which incur high costs and latency, or post-train a planner with reinforcement learning (RL) in a single domain, requiring a separate specialist for each domain with incompatible tools. In large language model (LLM) post-training, multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) has been used to consolidate domain specialists into a single generalist. Yet whether MOPD can build a generalist planner for agentic robotics, how well it performs, and how it compares with other consolidation methods remain unexplored. In this paper, we systematically study these questions: we introduce Robo-MOPD, which trains a single student on closed-loop rollouts in simulation under token-level supervision from matching frozen specialists, and compare it with weight merging, off-policy specialist supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and multi-domain online RL. Experiments on LIBERO-PRO and RoboCasa365 show that a single 9B Robo-MOPD planner reaches 72.9% and 44.8% success (58.9% average), surpassing all consolidated baselines in average success and both 9B specialists on their respective benchmarks. Robo-MOPD excels on long-horizon tasks, outperforming multi-domain online RL by 13.0 percentage points on LIBERO-10.

items.abstract: A relação entre gestão de pessoas, motivação e desempenho organizacional reúne evidências favoráveis, mas também resultados divergentes, o que exige análise dos mecanismos envolvidos. Este artigo analisa essas relações por meio de revisão narrativa, bibliográfica, qualitativa e exploratória de 18 artigos publicados entre 1995 e 2026, selecionados intencionalmente e examinados em cinco eixos temáticos. Os estudos apontam associações positivas entre sistemas integrados de gestão e desempenho, embora treinamento, avaliação e incentivos apresentem resultados variáveis conforme o contexto e os indicadores utilizados. Conclui-se que a articulação entre desenvolvimento, justiça, liderança e condições de trabalho oferece elementos para decisões gerenciais mais fundamentadas, sem autorizar inferências causais a partir desta revisão.

items.title: Guideline-based conversational artificial intelligence versus a web patient guideline before breast cancer surgery: a randomized controlled trial
items.abstract: Background Conversational artificial intelligence may help patients access guideline information before breast cancer surgery. We evaluated whether a guideline-based chatbot improved patient-reported shared decision-making compared with a web patient guideline. Methods In this single-center randomized controlled trial, adults with clinical stage 0–II breast cancer scheduled for surgery before systemic therapy received access to a chatbot or the web version of the same patient guideline during outpatient waiting time. Allocation was stratified by age and diagnosis before referral. The primary outcome was the 9-item Shared Decision-Making Questionnaire score (0–100) after the surgical decision. The primary comparison used a Welch t test on available outcomes in the assigned groups. Post hoc analyses included adjustment for allocation strata, multiple imputation in all randomized participants, and sensitivity analyses for missing outcomes. Results All 92 randomized participants initiated their allocated resource (46 per group). Primary outcomes were available for 38 chatbot and 42 web-guideline participants. Mean scores were 87.61 and 89.86, respectively (chatbot minus web guideline, − 2.25 points; 95% confidence interval − 8.27 to 3.77; P = 0.46). Multiple imputation gave a difference of − 1.79 points (95% confidence interval − 7.86 to 4.28). No secondary outcome showed a statistically discernible difference. Detailed use measures were available for 18 participants per group. A documented service interruption affected free-text chatbot responses during recruitment; menu-based access remained available. Conclusions The chatbot as delivered did not demonstrate added benefit for patient-reported shared decision-making over a web version of the same patient guideline. Missing outcomes, incomplete use measurements, and variable conversational availability limit interpretation; equivalence and the effect of a consistently functioning interface were not established. Evaluations of conversational access alongside existing guideline resources should measure incremental patient benefit and outcomes matched to its intended clinical function. items.title: How GenAI Can Undermine Its Own Productivity Gains: The Role of Technological Dependencies and Human Capabilities
items.abstract: Delegating a function to generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may produce an immediate productivity gain without securing the conditions required to sustain it. This conceptual article examines when delegation-induced changes in technological dependencies and the maintenance of human capabilities can affect subsequent productivity in the same business activity. Using theory adaptation, it combines an account of changed technological requirements with conditional antecedents concerning the organizational availability and maintenance of necessary human capabilities. The resulting proposition identifies two possible pathways: insufficient human capacity for routine evaluation, correction or exception handling despite normal GenAI service; and deterioration of a required technological contribution without adequate replacement. Either pathway affects productivity only where compensation is insufficient and the relationship between quality-consistent accepted output and predefined relevant real inputs worsens. Initial gains may persist, erode or disappear; observed productivity may also fall below its historical pre-delegation level. Such a historical reversal alone does not establish causation: erosion of the GenAI-attributable gain requires credible no-delegation comparisons for the relevant periods. Constructed comparisons illustrate these mechanisms, their boundary conditions and implications for capability maintenance and technological continuity.

items.title: How Organizational AI Ethics Governance Shapes Employee Creativity: A Conceptual Analysis of Mechanisms and Boundary Conditions
items.abstract: As AI becomes embedded in organizational decision-making and knowledge production, employees gain new tools for accessing and generating information while also confronting concerns about algorithmic evaluation, data use, and accountability. Drawing on research on AI ethics, algorithmic management, and organizational creativity, this conceptual study defines organizational AI ethics governance as the rules, procedures, and allocation of responsibilities that guide the development, deployment, operation, and retirement of AI systems. We argue that such governance can shape employee creativity through several connected mechanisms. Fair and contestable procedures can strengthen procedural justice, while transparent system boundaries and meaningful human review can support calibrated trust. Tolerance for responsible experimentation, together with discretion over how AI is used, can protect psychological safety and job autonomy. Governance also determines whether human–AI collaboration broadens exploration or channels employees toward standardized outputs. These effects depend on task characteristics, the stakes of AI-assisted decisions, whether AI is used primarily for automation or augmentation, employees' AI literacy, and the consistency between formal rules and managerial conduct. This study suggests that organizations should translate ethical principles into risk-based review, purpose limitation in data use, effective contestability and appeal mechanisms, employee participation, and oversight across the AI system life cycle so that AI can serve as a resource for careful creative work rather than a substitute for judgment.

items.title: How Systems Treat Intent: A Faceted Taxonomy of Intent for Human-AI Co-Creation
items.abstract: Human-AI interaction depends on systems acting on user intent rather than explicit procedures, even when that intent is incomplete, evolving, or partially communicable. Literature organizing systems by interaction technique, workflow stage, or division of labor, offer limited insight into which facet of intent an interaction mechanism addresses. We introduce a six-facet taxonomy of intent, grounded in philosophical accounts of mind, action, and meaning, and apply it to systems presented in 198 papers from eleven SIGCHI venues. Our analysis reveals that different forms of incomplete intent are associated with distinct interaction and authorship strategies, showing that mechanisms that appear similar often address fundamentally different intent-related problems. This exposes blind spots, as intent is rarely represented as an interaction object, authorship provenance is rarely tracked, and tentative preferences are rarely distinguished from firm commitments. The taxonomy offers a lens for analyzing and designing AI systems around the facets of intent they address.

items.title: How teachers refine and enact culturally situated STEAM worksheets drafted by generative AI for learning matrices in lesson study
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can now draft complete classroom materials, yet little is known about how such drafts fare once teachers refine and use them. This design-based study traced worksheets on matrices from an AI design prompt to classroom enactment in an Indonesian public upper secondary school. The worksheets combined an epistemic learning sequence with science, technology, engineering, arts, and mathematics (STEAM) contexts drawn from local culture. A model teacher taught them to 36 grade 11 students in four lesson study cycles observed by a second teacher and two researchers, and a conventionally taught class (n = 35) took the post-test for comparison. The confirmed worksheets conformed fully to only 6 of 48 coded prompt specifications. The lessons nonetheless sustained active participation, although written justification was often brief and largely missing in the final lesson, misconceptions appeared in two lessons, and unrendered notation had to be repaired by the teacher and by students. All students improved from pre-test to post-test (normalised gain = 0.55; d = 1.93), and the class outscored the comparison class (r = .49). Because the comparison class had no pre-test and some test content overlapped with the worksheets, these results indicate compatibility with learning rather than an effect. The value of AI-drafted materials depended on teachers’ decisions during confirmation and enactment.

items.title: Human Judgment in the Age of Algorithms: Decision Autonomy, Digital Oversight and Organizational Performance
items.abstract: Organizations that put algorithms into consequential decisions usually keep a person in the loop, on the assumption that the person adds something the model lacks. This paper checks that assumption against four bodies of published evidence: a meta-analysis of 106 experiments, field and trial evidence on judges, radiologists, physicians and consultants, a 2025 global survey of 1,993 respondents, and the oversight provisions of the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act. Published effects are put on a common scale and a short decision model is derived to show when an override can pay. On average a human–AI combination does worse than the better of its two members (Hedges’ g = − 0.23, 95% CI − 0.39 to − 0.07), which corresponds to a 43.5% chance of beating it. The loss is concentrated in decision tasks (g = − 0.27); in creation tasks the estimate is positive but imprecise (g = 0.19, CI − 0.09 to 0.48). Relative capability matters most: combinations gain when the human alone is the stronger member (g = 0.46) and lose when the algorithm is (g = − 0.54). In the model, unrestricted overrides change accuracy by exactly the accuracy gap between human and algorithm, and with unequal error costs the human’s odds of being right must exceed the algorithm’s by the cost ratio. In the survey, respondents at high-performing organizations were 2.8 times as likely to report a defined human-validation process (65% against 23%; odds ratio 6.2), an association that is large but cross-sectional and self-reported. The evidence is highly heterogeneous (I ² = 97.7%) and mostly predates current generative models. Oversight helps where it is built around what the human knows and the model does not, and not where it exists in name only.

items.title: Human-Centric Hyperautomation Using Supply Chain 5.0 Principles: A Front-Line Perspective
items.abstract: The Industry 4.0 focus upon digital transformation has evolved and shaped the notions of Society 5.0 and Supply Chain 5.0, shifting towards resilient, sustainable, and human-centric approaches. Confronted by the relentless advance of hyperautomation techniques, preserving the central role of humans is essential, not only to align with the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals, but also to optimise productivity and value creation. This paper explores the perceptions of front-line supply chain associates regarding the introduction of hyperautomation initiatives to identify approaches, benefits and challenges associated with achieving sustainable, Supply Chain 5.0-aligned, human-centric outcomes. Employing an inductive, phenomenological case study approach, data were gathered through a qualitative semi-structured survey of front-line associates across four business units within a UK-based, family-owned international logistics company and analysed using thematic analysis. The findings highlight challenges concerning employee hyperautomation-anxiety and trust associated with employer-employee communication, while revealing opportunities relating to job design, individual ambidexterity, higher-value work and human resource management. Drawing upon the personal perceptions of front-line associates exposed to hyperautomation initiatives, the paper offers a human-centric toolkit for Supply Chain 5.0, highlighting opportunities presented by skilling and job design to facilitate higher-value work, individual ambidexterity and increased productivity while addressing hyperautomation-anxiety. The research extends understanding of hyperautomation’s impact upon front-line supply chain associates and provides recommendations for future Supply Chain 5.0 policy and practice.

items.title: Integrating artificial intelligence into business management: implications for intellectual capital development
items.abstract: Purpose This study explores the implications of artificial intelligence (AI) integration into business management practices, emphasizing its impact on intellectual capital components. Specifically, it examines how AI integration influences the interaction between human, structural and relational capital in managerial processes. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a rigorous thematic analysis conducted in NVivo. Data collected through an online qualitative questionnaire administered to managers from multiple sectors were analyzed to identify key dimensions of AI integration in business contexts and to develop a conceptual model explaining their interactions. Findings The findings reveal four key dimensions: the role of AI in managerial processes, the challenges associated with AI, the strategies and best practices required to integrate AI into management and the strategies needed to adapt and train human resources in organizations integrating AI. While AI enhances efficiency, automation and decision-making processes, sustainable integration requires strategic planning, gradual implementation and investment in human capital. Overall, AI integration appears to enhance the interaction between human, structural and relational capital rather than radically restructuring intellectual capital. Practical implications The link between technological implementation and human-centered challenges provides practical guidance for organizations undergoing digital transformation. Gradual AI integration through pilot projects, employee training and governance structures supports responsible human–AI collaboration and strategic decision-making. Originality/value This research extends the traditional technology–organization–environment framework by conceptualizing AI integration as a dynamic socio-organizational process. Furthermore, it highlights how AI-driven managerial practices reinforce existing intellectual capital and provides a conceptual model explaining these dynamics.

items.title: Intelligent Cockpit Design through Coordination of Driving Tasks and Attentional Resources
items.abstract: The value of an intelligent cockpit depends on the fit between information, interaction modalities, and driving tasks. Drawing on an integrative analysis of design research, scenario-based design, attention, and human–automation interaction, this paper proposes a scenario–task–attention–initiative framework. Scenarios are translated into tasks with explicit responsibility, timing, and consequence constraints. Modality selection is treated as a resource-competition problem, while proactive system behavior is bounded by uncertainty, authorization, and recovery conditions. Event-level evidence from use feeds back into problem framing and AI-assisted design. The contribution is a conceptual model operationalized as an analytical design method: an event record links task constraints, admissible service actions, and revisions to design assumptions. Comparisons with four theoretical foundations identify inherited mechanisms and proposed relationships. Worked scenario and task cards, a qualitative decision procedure, and four operationalized propositions make the synthesis inspectable. No driving experiment was conducted; its incremental benefits, classification reliability, and safety implications remain to be empirically tested.

items.title: Intelligent Transformation Readiness and Workforce Allocation in Chinese Listed Firms
items.abstract: This study examines the relationships between readiness for intelligent transformation, AI-related activities, and firms’ labor allocation. Drawing on sociotechnical systems theory and a task-based perspective, it combines annual reports and recruitment data from Chinese A-share listed firms. It constructs a composite readiness index, classifies AI application mentions by business scenario and technological capability, and estimates models with firm and year fixed effects. The capability regressions cover 35,701 firm-year observations and retain zero counts. Cognitive AI disclosure counts are positively associated with the high-skilled employee share and negatively associated with the medium- and low-skilled shares. Compared with cognitive AI, perceptual AI has coefficients of opposite sign for the high- and low-skilled shares and a negative coefficient closer to zero for the medium-skilled share. The estimated coefficients for cognitive AI differ significantly from those for both perceptual and behavioral AI across all three skill shares. The preferred fixed-effects Poisson models show that higher readiness is associated with lower demand for routine jobs and higher demand for non-routine jobs overall and non-routine cognitive jobs. Baseline models associate higher readiness with lower medium-skilled and higher low-skilled shares. However, these findings are limited to conditional associations at the share level and do not extend to log-ratio specifications. These conditional associations provide firm-level evidence on workforce skill composition across different AI capabilities and recruitment demand across task categories. The findings suggest that understanding labor allocation in intelligent transformation requires distinguishing among technology measures and dimensions of labor outcomes.

items.title: Interrogation Protocols for AI Control
items.abstract: As the intelligence of an AI agent increases relative to a trusted monitor, so does the risk that the monitor will fail to understand the agent's actions or to evaluate them confidently. We introduce interrogation protocols to a high-stakes AI control setting, and allow the monitor to ask the untrusted agent questions about confusing actions. For interrogation to improve safety, a weaker model must be able to distinguish misleading explanations produced by an attack policy from genuine ones produced by an honest policy. We find that on a held-out subset of BashArena, an interrogation protocol improves safety at a 1% audit budget from 72.6% for an actions-only baseline, which does not use interrogations, to 79.5% (+7.0 pp [+0.9, +20.1], 95% paired bootstrap interval), but most of this uplift can be captured by having a trusted model state a specific concern. More broadly, our work suggests that interrogating agents can improve safety, allowing monitors to catch more attacks at a larger capability gap.

items.title: Is assessment design encouraging AI offloading?
items.abstract: Generative AI has ended the assumption that unsupervised student work reflects a student’s own unaided thinking, forcing a return to first principles in assessment. This article uses The University of Sydney’s two-lane approach, which separates secure assessment of learning from open assessment for and as learning, to frame a practical account of putting AI into students’ hands. Drawing on ‘Dr MattTabolism’, an AI biochemistry tutor I built and deployed, and on a computational study of how students actually used it, I show a consistent gap between how such tools are designed and how they are used. Students largely sought answers rather than sustained dialogue, satisfaction did not correlate with improved learning outcomes, and usage concentrated around deadlines. How educators contextualised AI use affected learning more than how the tool behaved. I argue that this offloading is partly a product of over-assessment, and that formative, lower-stakes work remains essential precisely because it is where students can afford the desirable difficulties that learning requires. Reducing assessment load is a validity measure, not a soft option. I close with practical starting points for educators, framed around the pedagogical roles AI can play and the risks each carries, and the educator’s role as designer.

items.title: L’intelligence artificielle au service du contrôle de gestion : une revue systématique de la littérature
items.abstract: Cet article examine comment l’intelligence artificielle (IA) transforme le contrôle de gestion, selon trois axes : les mécanismes de la transformation, les conditions organisationnelles qui en déterminent l’efficacité et l’évolution du rôle du contrôleur de gestion. Une revue systématique de la littérature conduite selon le protocole PRISMA 2020 a permis de retenir 39 articles issus de Scopus et de Google Scholar, publiés entre 2015 et 2026, analysés au moyen d’une matrice de synthèse et d’une analyse thématique transversale. Les résultats mettent en évidence six mécanismes : l’automatisation, l’analytique augmentée, l’intelligence prédictive, l’aide à la décision, le pilotage en temps réel et l’apprentissage organisationnel. Ils identifient quatre conditions organisationnelles : la qualité et la gouvernance des données, les compétences analytiques et numériques, une culture managériale fondée sur les données et la gouvernance de l’IA. La relation entre IA et performance organisationnelle apparaît indirecte et conditionnelle, le contrôle de gestion jouant vraisemblablement un rôle de médiation qui reste à tester, tandis que le rôle du contrôleur évolue vers l’interprétation, l’anticipation et l’aide à la décision. L’article formalise ces résultats dans un modèle intégrateur assorti de six propositions de recherche et propose un agenda de recherche.

items.title: Learning Cannot Be Delegated: Why the Division of Cognitive Work Between Learners and Generative AI Should Shift Over Time
items.abstract: The promise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in education has motivated a rapidly growing literature whose titles, abstracts, and keywords mention acceptance, attitudes, intention, or perception more than six times as often as self-regulated learning or metacognition. This critical review argues that research on GenAI in education is repeating the founding mistake of learning analytics, measuring what is easy to count rather than what matters for learning. Building on the COPES model of self-regulated learning, this paper develops the gradual reduction of AI delegation (GRAD) framework, in which GenAI performs, proposes, or prompts at eight task stages. Within GRAD, GenAI can take on operations essential to the learning goal. Such delegation helps rather than replaces learning only when the support fades as learners improve. For claims that GenAI improves learning, the paper proposes four validity criteria, namely unassisted outcomes, process evidence, calibration, and ideally gains that outlast the support.

items.title: Learning Personalized Human Driving Strategies for Negotiation With Automated Vehicles via Inverse Reinforcement Learning and a Hybrid Markov Decision Process
items.abstract: As human-driven vehicles (HVs) and automated vehicles (AVs) increasingly share public roads, AVs must anticipate how human drivers negotiate right-of-way conflicts. Using 648 simulator trials across 6 competitive HV–AV scenarios, we apply maximum-entropy inverse reinforcement learning to recover scenario-specific reward structures representing efficiency, safety, and comfort. We then train a lightweight hybrid Markov decision process policy through behavior cloning followed by reward-based fine-tuning. The hybrid model achieves lower average displacement error than behavior-cloning-only and reinforcement-learning-only baselines across all scenario groups. A separate outcome head predicts whether the human-driven vehicle or AV will proceed first from partial trajectories. Participant characteristics are incorporated only through post-hoc calibration of the outcome-prediction threshold, while reward and control-policy learning remain scenario-level. Accuracy, F1, and AUC improve as more interaction context becomes available, and participant-aware calibration provides modest early prediction benefits in scenarios where the interaction state is sufficiently informative.
